Kentucky Pedestrian and Bike Data Portal

User guide

Open the data portal

The Kentucky Pedestrian and Bike Data Portal provides a central repository for pedestrian and bike related data available in Kentucky. It is intended to support pedestrian and bike data sharing in Kentucky and advance related practice and research to promote pedestrian and bike travel and safety.

What's in the portal

The portal can be accessed via this link: Kentucky Pedestrian and Bike Data Portal. As of September 2026, the portal contains the following data:

  • Simulated daily pedestrian volume (via the synthetic household-level travel demand model, see technical memo for more details);
  • Simulated daily pedestrian trip production and attraction at census block level (via the same model as above);
  • Simulated daily bike volume (via the same model as above);
  • Simulated daily bike trip production and attraction at census block level (via the same model as above);
  • Observed pedestrian and bike counts collected by consultants working on corridor study for the Kentucky Transportation Cabinet;
  • Pedestrian and bike crashes from 2019 to 2023, displayed as crash hot spots when the corresponding layer is enabled.

About the simulated data

Note that the simulated volumes and trip demands represent default parameters used by the synthetic model that are not yet calibrated with Kentucky-specific walk and bike activity data. Their accuracy has not been objectively evaluated; therefore, they should be treated as proxy indicators of pedestrian and bicycle exposure rather than validated observed counts.

Also, Streetlight pedestrian and bike average daily traffic (ADT) data is not made publicly available here due to data sharing restrictions.

Finding your way around

The screenshot below shows the layout of the portal, including the toolbar on the left side of the map viewer, allowing users to click on Layers for switching display of map layers, and Legend to show the symbology of active layers. Users can use Bookmarks to move to a pre-set geographic area such as Louisville, Lexington, Northern Kentucky, Bowling Green, Paducah, and Ashland.

To zoom in to a particular place, users can click on the Search icon located on the lower right corner of the page and type in an address in the popped-up text window.

Showing and hiding layers

Within the Layers panel, layer groups can be expanded to show the individual pedestrian, bicycle, count, and crash layers. Users can hover over a particular layer to turn on or off the display of that layer.

Pedestrian and bike volumes

Use the Pedestrian ADT or Bike ADT layer to view simulated daily pedestrian or bicycle volume along roadway segments. The line symbology represents volume classes, whose value ranges can be seen by clicking on Legend. Both Pedestrian ADT and Bike ADT layers have visible labels when they are zoomed to street block level, as shown below. For streets with sidewalks, both mainline lines (typically having zero pedestrian volume) and sidewalk lines (used by pedestrians passing through that street) are displayed on the map.

The Geography Detail layer can be activated when viewing non-roadway network layers to provide more context such as highways, roads, and administrative boundaries.

Trip origins and destinations

The census-block layers show simulated origins and destinations of walking and bicycle trips. They are useful for comparing where simulated pedestrian or bicycle travel demand is generated versus where trips are attracted.

Observed counts

The portal also hosts a layer displaying the locations where pedestrian and/or bike counts were collected as part of the turning movement counts for KYTC corridor studies. These counts were collected at different dates and times of day with varying durations. They can be converted into ADTs with adjustment factors derived from credible continuous counts once such data becomes available.

Crash hot spots

The PedBike_Crashes_2019_2023 group contains separate pedestrian and bicycle crash layers for 2019 through 2023. When one of these layers is enabled, the map displays the hot spots of the crashes. The pedestrian crash heatmap in the Lexington area is shown below.

These crash layers can help identify locations with concentrations of reported pedestrian or bicycle crashes during 2019–2023. The portal includes these data as an additional proxy indicator related to pedestrian and bicycle activity exposure.

Guide current as of September 2026.
